extracted.intended_audience: students, critics, and practitioners of poetry, drama, and rhetorical prose (writers, dramatists, literary critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging poetry, tragic drama, rhetoric, and prose style drawn from Aristotle's Poetics, Longinus' On the Sublime, and Demetrius' On Style. Covers plot, character, diction, rhetorical figures, rhythm, and the aesthetic effect on an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of plot
rubrics_metrics.description: “a plot must have unity, it must be one story, not several” (Aristotle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful tragedy or narrative should present a single coherent action with connected incidents; avoid multiple unconnected subplots. Unity promotes clarity and the intended emotional effect (e.g., catharsis). Anti-pattern: scattering attention over several independent stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate narrative length
rubrics_metrics.description: “it must not be so long that the audience forgets the beginning before it is ended.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the action compact enough for the audience to retain its structure and effects; avoid unnecessary prolongation. Long, diffuse narratives dilute emotional impact and thematic coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic hero: cause but not desert of fate (hamartia)
rubrics_metrics.description: the hero must be “heroic” and must cause his fate but not deserve it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tragic protagonist should be noble or elevated and must make an error or experience a misstep that produces catastrophe; the audience must perceive the misfortune as arising from a plausible mistake rather than deserved moral corruption. Anti-pattern: a wholly villainous or wholly blameless protagonist who fails to generate tragic pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot over psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: “psychology must be subordinate to plot.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character motivations and psychological detail should serve the requirements and movement of the plot rather than supplanting structural necessity. The sequence of events and causal mechanics of the action are primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus integration
rubrics_metrics.description: “the chorus must play its part in the action.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In drama (classical context) any collective or recurring element must be functionally integrated into the plot and not merely decorative; avoid choruses or recurring sections that interrupt rather than advance action or theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: catharsis (purge of emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry (especially tragic drama) affords “the pleasure of having one’s emotions stirred” and acts as a medicine to purge pent-up emotion (katharsis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art’s value lies partly in its capacity to arouse and then purify emotion in the audience; design scenes and arcs to produce pity, fear, and release, rather than merely sensationalism. Anti-pattern: emotional manipulation without form or purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as imitation of universal truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry records “not what did happen but what would happen” and thereby reveals universal principles (Aristotle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good literary art represents general truths about human nature and action rather than merely chronicling particulars. Emphasize structured, exemplary incidents that illuminate universal causal relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of representation (medium-specific elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different arts differ “either in using means generically different or in representing different objects or in representing objects not in the same way.” Means include rhythm, language, tune, metre, gesture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match technique to medium: use rhythm/tune for music and dance, language and metre for poetry, and combined means for drama. Choose artistic means appropriate to the expressive goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character types and genre: better/worse/like us
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters represented are either “better than ourselves or worse or much what we are”; tragedy tends to represent better, comedy worse, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select character moral stature deliberately according to genre conventions—tragic heroes elevated; comic characters satirically inferior; mimic/normal characters for certain mimes or dialogues. Anti-pattern: mismatching character moral level and genre expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of representation (narrative vs. dramatic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation may be “partly by narrative and partly by assuming a character” (Homer’s method) or by remaining oneself, or by having characters enact the action themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to tell, impersonate, or dramatize; each mode affects immediacy and audience engagement. Use combination deliberately (e.g., epic narrative with embedded speeches) and be consistent with genre aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic diction: balance of strange and ordinary words
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet uses “a judicious mixture of strange and ordinary words” so that he is both intelligible and ‘poetic.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend elevated and common diction to achieve freshness without opacity. Overuse of archaisms or rarities becomes jargon; too much ordinariness loses poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of metre and form to naming (genre labels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work is often named by metre (epic, elegiac), though the 'poet' label properly attaches to the act of representation rather than metre alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that formal choices (metre, combined metres) shape audience expectations and genre identity; use formal features intentionally rather than by convention alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity measured by audience absorption/illusion
rubrics_metrics.description: For Longinus the chief test of excellence is “the absorption or illusion (éxoracs) of the audience or reader” — the capacity to engross and elevate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sublime or elevated writing by its power to transport and fully engage the audience; succeeded sublimity leaves a strong, memorable emotional/ intellectual impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity arises from personality and sincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: “Style is the shadow of a personality” and grandeur (the sublime) comes from a forceful human character and genuine feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate an authentic, vigorous voice and sincere feeling; rhetorical virtuosity without inner conviction cannot produce true sublimity. Anti-pattern: ornate surface with vacuous sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures/tropes as means not ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Longinus and Demetrius stress that tropes, figures, and technical devices are “only means of analysis” and should serve genuine feeling or content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhetorical figures (metaphor, personification, anaphora, etc.) to enhance expression and effect; avoid ornament that draws attention to itself and obscures meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain style virtues: clarity, naturalness, vividness
rubrics_metrics.description: Demetrius praises the plain style for its “natural expression” and vividness; short, simple phrasing suits passion and conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For subjects requiring sincerity or everyday character, favor straightforward diction, short phrases, and concrete detail. Anti-patterns: affected elegance or overwrought ornament in subjects that need directness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevated style devices and cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: The elevated style employs metaphor, compound words, long syllables, vowel harmony and musical effects to achieve grandeur; but misuse causes frigidity and artificiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply elevated devices (bold metaphors, weighty compounds, harmonious sound patterns) to match noble subject matter, but avoid excess that produces coldness or obscurity. Usage and taste should moderate daring experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forcible style: rugged diction and concentrated phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: A forcible style relies on rugged or emphatic words, compact phrases, and rhythmic strength to produce impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use terse, forceful lexical choices and compact phrasing for argumentative or invective contexts. Beware of aridity if phrasing becomes too curtailed.

rubrics_metrics.name: The period and sentence structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition and management of the period: number and length of members, simple vs composite periods; combination of periodic and running styles is recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary sentence architecture (periodic vs running) to suit rhetorical aims: periodic sentences produce deliberate, formal effect; running sentences yield ease and continuity. Avoid excessive uniformity or overly long members that obscure comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm and cadences in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose has rhythmical elements analogous to verse; metrical cadences should be used with caution and points of rhythm raised for effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to sound, cadence, and prosody in prose to produce verbal music, but do not force metrical patterns that make prose sing-songy or artificial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of diction and tone to subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Match language to subject matter (e.g., Megarian/Dorian claims about 'action' and local linguistic habits), and generally suit tone and diction to theme and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose plain or elevated diction, rhythm, and figures according to the seriousness, scope, and cultural context of the subject. Mismatch undermines credibility and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor and simile: discriminating use
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor contributes to elevation when used with discrimination; Demetrius discusses convertible vs non-convertible metaphors and the expansion of metaphor into simile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphors that illuminate and surprise without straining plausibility; expand metaphors into similes where appropriate to clarify and amplify. Anti-pattern: mixed or over-extended metaphors that confuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usage as arbiter (conservative authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Usage, as the sovereign arbiter” — customary usage guides acceptability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect linguistic and stylistic conventions as the final judge of what is readable and acceptable; innovation must still be intelligible to users/readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vividness through concrete detail and imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain style's essential element is vividness — use of concrete, sensory detail to create immediacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ precise images and particulars to animate scenes and characters; avoid abstraction when vividness is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound and phonetic effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of vowel harmony, long syllables, consonance, onomatopoeia, and other sound effects contributes to elevation and vividness (but avoid overuse in plain style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate attention to phonetics—long/short syllables, vowel combinations, and consonantal patterns—can heighten effect. Over-concentration of similar sounds risks monotony or artificiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding obscurity and frigidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscurity usually harms comprehension, though occasionally it can paradoxically increase force; frigidity arises from over-elaborate, unnatural ornamentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clarity and naturalness; if employing obscurity for effect, do so consciously and sparingly. Avoid rhetorical devices that produce cold, lifeless language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and inner meaning over mere technique
rubrics_metrics.description: “Without that [genuine feeling] no skill in writing is of value and its presence covers a multitude of faults.” Style should reflect a mind full of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize authentic thought and feeling; technical mastery should serve and reveal inner conviction rather than substitute for it. Anti-pattern: technical virtuosity devoid of substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy: what is omitted matters
rubrics_metrics.description: According to Demetrius (and Theophrastus’s view cited), distinction of style lies as much in what is omitted as in what is said.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be economical; strategic omission can increase force and elegance. Avoid unnecessary elaboration that weakens focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and proverb for effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition can be used for effect or clarity; proverbs and familiar sayings add weight when apt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ repetition and traditional sayings judiciously to emphasize or make connections; avoid mechanical redundancy that bores the reader.
